1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m leaning to C, First and third.

The reason the croisé / épaulement framing keeps coming up is because in Vaganova the four arabesques en arrière are taught as two families, not four separate leg positions. The odd-numbered arabesques are the croisé/opposition family and the even-numbered are the effacé family.

Arabesque I is the classic en arrière cambré. The torso is opened on the long diagonal and the port de bras is one arm porté en avant and one arm porté en arrière in a straight line with the body. The arm that is carried forward is the standing-leg arm, i.e. on the contralateral / opposite side to the lifted leg, with the back arm on the same side as the working leg. That one arm in front opposite the leg, the other back with the leg, is the textbook Vaganova opposition line and it is taught as the defining port de bras of I.

Arabesque III keeps exactly that same contralateral relationship, just with a more pronounced épaulement and a higher, more horizontal port de bras. The body is turned away from the working leg, but the leading arm that is extended en avant remains on the side of the supporting leg, so it is still opposite the lifted leg, and the back arm remains on the side of the lifted leg. It is the higher, more open development of the I line, not a both-arms-forward position.

The even-numbered arabesques are the other family. Arabesque II is taught effacé with the arms kept more in seconde and the front arm carried toward the same side as the lifted leg rather than in the classic contralateral opposition. Arabesque IV is the closed / more en face variation where the arm line stays nearer to the torso and the characteristic single contralateral forward arm is not the defining feature.

That is why the “single arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg” quality is the defining port de bras of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, I and III, in Vaganova.

4.text:
C. First and third.

The four Vaganova arabesques en arrière are distinguished by épaulement / port de bras, not by leg height alone. The croisé / opposition diagonal is the odd-numbered family.

* Arabesque I – classic cambré / croisé en arrière. The torso is opened on a long diagonal, the body is in profile and the arms are placed in opposition in a straight line with the body. The arm porté en avant is the arm on the side of the standing / supporting leg, i.e. contralateral to the lifted leg, and the arm porté en arrière is on the same side as the working leg. That is the textbook “one arm forward opposite the leg, one arm back with the leg” line.

* Arabesque III – the higher, more open development of the same croisé principle. Épaulement is more pronounced and the port de bras is higher / more horizontal, but the relationship is retained: the forward arm remains on the supporting-leg side, opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm remaining on the side of the lifted leg. It is the higher continuation of I, not a both-arms-forward position.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the even-numbered effacé family. II is taught effacé with the arms essentially in seconde / a more symmetrical line and the forward arm carried toward the same side as the lifted leg rather than in true contralateral opposition. IV is the closed / en face variation with the arms brought more in unison / low first / fifth and the characteristic single opposite-side forward arm is not the defining feature.

Hence the defining contralateral “arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg” port de bras is the defining feature of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, I and III.

11.text:
C. First and third

The four standing arabesques en arrière in Vaganova are a port de bras / épaulement series. The defining “one arm en avant on the side of the standing leg, one arm en arrière on the side of the working leg” line is the croisé / opposition family, and in Vaganova’s numbering that family is the odd-numbered arabesques.

* Arabesque I is the classic cambré / en arrière en croix. The torso is opened on a long diagonal and the arms are placed in a straight line with the body, one arm porté en avant on the supporting-leg side and one arm porté en arrière on the working-leg side. The forward arm is therefore carried contralaterally, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the leg. That is the textbook Vaganova opposition counterbalance.

* Arabesque III keeps the same croisé opposition relationship as I. The épaulement is more pronounced and the port de bras is higher / more horizontal, the torso is turned away from the working leg, but the arm that is brought en avant is still the standing-leg arm, so it remains on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm retained on the same side as the leg. It is the higher, more open continuation of the I line.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the even-numbered effacé / closed family. II is taught effacé with the arms essentially more in seconde and the front arm not in the classic contralateral opposition line, and IV is the closed / en face variation where the arm line stays nearer to the torso and the single opposite-side forward arm is not the defining feature. Hence the arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg is the defining port de bras of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques I and III.

3.text:
C. First and third

The four Vaganova arabesques en arrière are a port de bras / épaulement series on the same basic leg line. The odd-numbered arabesques are the croisé / opposition family and the even-numbered arabesques are the effacé / closed family.

Arabesque I is the classic cambré/en arrière croisé. The torso is opened on a long diagonal with épaulement and the arms are placed in a straight line with the body, one arm porté en avant and one arm porté en arrière. The arm that is carried en avant is the arm on the side of the standing/supporting leg, i.e. contralateral/opposite to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the working leg. That is the textbook Vaganova contralateral front-arm line.

Arabesque III keeps the same croisé opposition relationship as I, with a more pronounced épaulement and a higher/more horizontal port de bras. The torso is turned away from the working leg, the line remains elongated on a long diagonal, and the forward arm remains on the supporting-leg side, therefore still opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm retained on the same side as the leg. It is the higher, more open development of the I line.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the even-numbered effacé variations. II is taught effacé with the arms more in seconde / a more closed line and the forward arm is not placed in the classic single contralateral opposition; IV is the closed, more en face variation where the port de bras is brought forward in unison and the characteristic single opposite-side forward arm is lost.

Hence the defining “one arm extended in front on the side opposite the lifted leg, the other arm back on the same side as the leg” port de bras is the defining feature of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, Arabesque I and Arabesque III.

6.text:
C. First and third.

The four Vaganova standing arabesques en arrière are a port de bras / épaulement family, not four different leg lines.

The odd-numbered arabesques are the croisé / opposition family.

* Arabesque I is the classic cambré / en arrière croisé. The torso is elongated on a long diagonal, the working leg is derrière and the port de bras is one arm porté en avant on the side of the standing leg and one arm porté en arrière on the same side as the working leg. The arm that is carried en avant is therefore contralateral to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the leg. That is the textbook Vaganova “one arm forward opposite the leg, one arm back with the leg” line.

* Arabesque III is the same croisé opposition principle with a different épaulement / degree of opening and a higher, more horizontal port de bras. The torso is turned away from the working leg with a more pronounced épaulement, but the arm which is brought en avant is still the standing-leg arm, i.e. on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the other arm en arrière on the side of the lifted leg. It is the higher, more open development of the I line.

The even-numbered arabesques are the effacé / closed family.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are taught with the arms more symmetrical / essentially in seconde and with a more closed épaulement. The forward arm is not placed in the classic contralateral opposition line; the arms are kept more to the side or in a more unison forward line, so a single arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg is not the defining port de bras of those two positions.

Hence the defining “arm extended in front on the opposite side as the lifted leg” quality belongs to the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, first and third.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. First and third

The four standing arabesques are a port de bras / épaulement series on the same en arrière leg line. In Vaganova the odd-numbered positions are the croisé / opposition family and the even-numbered positions are the effacé / closed family.

Arabesque I is the classic en arrière cambré / croisé arabesque. The torso is opened on a long diagonal, essentially in profile, and the port de bras is one arm porté en avant and one arm porté en arrière in a straight line with the body. The arm that is carried en avant is the arm on the side of the standing/supporting leg, i.e. contralateral to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the working leg. That is the textbook Vaganova contralateral front-arm opposition line.

Arabesque III is the higher, more open development of the same croisé opposition principle. The épaulement is more pronounced and the port de bras is higher/more horizontal, but the relationship to the leg is unchanged: the front arm remains on the supporting-leg side, therefore opposite the lifted leg, and the back arm remains on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the higher/open version of I, not a both-arms-forward position.

Arabesque II and Arabesque IV are the even-numbered effacé variations. The forward arm is not placed in the classic contralateral opposition; in II the arms are kept more in a second/effacé line and the front arm is essentially on the same side as the lifted leg, and IV is the closed/low first position with the arms brought in unison nearer the torso. Neither even position is defined by a single arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg in the way I and III are.

The “one arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the other arm back on the same side as the leg” contralateral port de bras is therefore the defining feature of the odd-numbered croisé opposition arabesques, I and III. The minority description of I as bras en deux / no arm forward and of II as the classic opposition is best read as a naming conflation with Cecchetti/Ballet Imperial numbering, where the croisé family is often labeled II/III. On Vaganova’s own numbering the contralateral front-arm quality belongs to I and III.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. First and third.

I’m staying with the odd-numbered croisé / opposition pair, and I think the push for B Second and third is mixing up the Vaganova port de bras labels with the way the positions are sometimes described in notes.

In Vaganova the four arabesques en arrière are taught as a port de bras / épaulement series, not just as leg heights.

* Arabesque I is the classic cambré en arrière croisé. The torso is opened on a long diagonal and the arms are placed in opposition, one arm porté en avant and one arm porté en arrière in a straight line with the body. 3.text:
C. First and third

In Vaganova the four standing arabesques en arrière are a port de bras / épaulement series. The odd-numbered positions are the croisé / opposition family and the even-numbered positions are the effacé / closed family.

* Arabesque I is the classic cambré / en arrière croisé. The torso is opened on a long diagonal, the body is in profile, and the port de bras is in strict opposition: one arm porté en avant on the side of the standing/supporting leg and one arm porté en arrière on the side of the working leg. The arm carried en avant is therefore contralateral, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the leg.

* Arabesque III keeps that same croisé opposition relationship. The épaulement is more pronounced and the port de bras is higher / more horizontal and more open, but the leading arm that is extended en avant remains the standing-leg arm, so it remains on the side opposite the lifted leg, with the back arm retained on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the higher, more open development of the I line.

Arabesque II is the effacé variation with the arms essentially in / near seconde, more symmetrical/closed, and the forward arm not placed in the classic contralateral opposition. Arabesque IV is the closed / en face variation with the port de bras brought in toward the torso and the characteristic single opposite-side forward arm lost.

The defining “one arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the other arm back on the same side as the leg” port de bras is therefore the defining feature of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, Arabesque I and Arabesque III.

Torso opened on a long diagonal in profile, arms placed in strict opposition in a straight line with the body: one arm porté en avant on the standing/supporting-leg side and one arm porté en arrière on the working-leg side. The forward arm is therefore contralateral, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the leg. This is the textbook Vaganova contralateral front-arm opposition line.

Arabesque III keeps the same croisé opposition relationship as I, developed higher/more open with more pronounced épaulement and a higher, more horizontal/more open port de bras. The forward arm remains the standing-leg arm, still opposite the lifted leg, and the back arm remains on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the higher continuation of the I line, not a both-arms-forward position.

Arabesque II is the even-numbered effacé variation: upper body more square, arms essentially in/near seconde, more symmetrical/closed, forward arm not placed in classic contralateral opposition, often carried more toward the same side as the lifted leg.

Arabesque IV is the closed / en face variation: port de bras brought in toward the torso / low first / fifth, more closed épaulement, the characteristic single opposite-side forward arm lost.

Important claims retained: the “arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg” quality is the defining port de bras of the croisé opposition pair; port de bras changes, leg line does not; opposition = croisé = odd numbers in Vaganova numbering.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. First and third

In Vaganova the four standing arabesques en arrière are taught as two port de bras / épaulement families on the same leg line.

The odd-numbered arabesques are the croisé / opposition family; the even-numbered are the effacé / closed family. It is this family membership that gives the single front arm on the opposite side to the lifted leg.

Arabesque I is the classic cambré / en arrière croisé. The torso is opened on a long diagonal in profile with épaulement and the arms are placed in strict opposition in line with the body: one arm porté en avant on the standing/supporting-leg side and one arm porté en arrière on the working-leg side. The forward arm is therefore carried contralaterally, i.e. on the opposite side of the body to the lifted leg, with the back arm ipsilateral to the leg.

Arabesque III keeps exactly that same contralateral opposition relationship. The épaulement is more pronounced and the port de bras is higher / more horizontal and more open, but the arm relationship to the leg is unchanged: the arm brought en avant remains the standing-leg arm, so it stays on the side opposite the lifted leg, and the back arm remains on the same side as the lifted leg. It is the higher, more open development of the I line.

Arabesque II is the effacé variation with the arms more in/near seconde and symmetrical; the forward arm is not placed in the classic contralateral opposition. Arabesque IV is the closed / en face variation where the port de bras is brought more in unison toward the torso and the characteristic single opposite-side forward arm is lost.

Hence the defining “one arm extended in front on the opposite side to the lifted leg, the other arm back on the same side as the leg” port de bras is the defining feature of the odd-numbered croisé arabesques, First and Third.

Current belief is strongly C First and third. All 12 colleagues are now publicly unanimous on C in round 4, up from unanimous C after round 2. Round 4 reasoning is fully convergent on the two-family framing:

* Vaganova’s four arabesques are taught on the same leg line as two port de bras/épaulement families: odd-numbered croisé/opposition = I and III; even-numbered effacé/closed = II and IV.

* Arabesque I = classic cambré/en arrière croisé. Torso opened on long diagonal in profile with épaulement. * Arabesque II = even-numbered effacé. Arms more in/near seconde, more symmetrical/closed, forward arm not placed in classic contralateral opposition.

* Arabesque IV = closed/en face/low first variation. Port de bras brought in unison toward torso, characteristic single opposite-side forward arm lost.

Persistent minority concern preserved from earlier rounds: alternative naming systems map the contralateral opposition to Vaganova II/III.
